claims.text: Thin, epitaxial oxide coatings designed using DFT-guided atomistic interface simulations can significantly enhance the oxidation resistance of reactive metal systems.
The uncoated substrate is prone to rapid oxidation at high temperature.
The substrate forms non-protective oxide scales under high-temperature conditions.
A 5–10 nm epitaxial oxide coating selected and optimized through DFT is an appropriate oxidation-resistance intervention.
Approximately 1000 K is representative of the intended high-temperature service conditions.
Engineering the substrate/coating interface can minimize interfacial defects.
Engineering the substrate/coating interface can ensure coherent bonding.
The designed oxide layer forms a stable, low-defect interfacial bond with the substrate.
A stable, low-defect coating/substrate interface reduces oxygen diffusion.
Reduced oxygen diffusion inhibits the formation of deleterious oxide scales.
An optimal coating electronic structure supports formation of a thermodynamically stable protective layer.
The coated substrate will have a markedly lower oxidation rate than an uncoated substrate under the stated conditions.
The coated substrate will retain its mechanical properties better than an uncoated substrate under the stated conditions.
Rapid formation of non-protective oxide scales on an uncoated substrate leads to performance degradation.
The method succeeds only when the substrate is compatible with the epitaxial oxide coating.
The method is limited to a temperature range near 1000 K in which the designed interface remains stable.
Interfacial mechanical compatibility may vary with substrate composition.
